proposed.text: A building owner asks whether PD 1096 distinguishes between a 'Certificate of Occupancy' for new buildings and a separate 'Certificate of Use' for changes of use in existing buildings. What is the correct position under the Code?

options.text: PD 1096 does distinguish the two: the Certificate of Occupancy is for new construction and the Certificate of Use is for approved changes of use in existing buildings

PD 1096 recognizes only the Certificate of Occupancy. Under Sec. 309(c) an approved change of use triggers issuance of a new Certificate of Occupancy; there is no separate 'Certificate of Use' instrument in the Code
The Certificate of Occupancy is issued by the City Mayor, while the Certificate of Use is issued by the Building Official under a separate procedural track
'Certificate of Use' is the informal, interchangeable term for the Certificate of Occupancy when applied to existing buildings

rationale.a: Fabricates a separate 'Certificate of Use' that does not exist in PD 1096; this is the most common change-of-use trap.
rationale.c: Misstates the issuer and invents a parallel procedural track; only the Building Official issues the Certificate of Occupancy under Sec. 308-309.
rationale.d: Treats the fabricated term as a harmless synonym; PD 1096's sole instrument is the Certificate of Occupancy, and using 'Certificate of Use' as a synonym perpetuates a non-existent distinction.
rationale.correct: PD 1096 issues only one post-completion authorization: the Certificate of Occupancy. Section 309(c) of the 2004 Revised IRR (Sec. 309.9) provides that no change may be made in the existing use or occupancy classification of a building or portion thereof until the Building Official has issued a new Certificate of Occupancy for it. A change of use therefore produces a fresh Certificate of Occupancy - not a different document. The 'Certificate of Use' is a fabricated term with no basis in PD 1096.
rationale.takeaway: Reject any answer that splits occupancy authorization into two PD 1096 instruments. The Code has only the Certificate of Occupancy; Sec. 309(c) covers changes of use via a new Certificate of Occupancy.
